bibl.title: A computational model of anterior cingulate function in speeded response tasks: Effects of frequency, sequence, and conflict

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: The results indicate that the conflict-monitoring hypothesis, augmented by mechanisms for encoding stimulus history, can explain key phenomena associated with performance in sequential speeded response tasks.

span.label: response conflict monitoring in anterior cingulate cortex
span.quote: Specifically, we have hypothesized that the function of the ACC is to provide an on-line index of the degree of response conflict.

span.label: simulation
span.quote: Simulations conducted in a neural network model incorporating sequential priming mechanisms (developed in Cho et al., 2002) confirmed that a computational measure of response conflict was higher on low-frequency trials across all three tasks.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Repeated high-frequency stimuli build residual activation (an expectancy) in one stimulus-response pathway, so a low-frequency stimulus must overcome that preactivation, and the resulting competition is what registers as conflict in ACC.
span.quote: Specifically, in the model, repeated presentations of high-frequency stimuli create an expectancy for continued future repetitions, which results in residual activity in the expected stimulus– response pathway.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Conflict at the decision layer produces ACC-indexed signal that lowers strategic priming, which raises control (slower, more accurate responding) on subsequent trials.
span.quote: The role of the conflict detector was to increase control by decreasing strategic priming in response to conflict.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because the incorrect nontarget decision unit in one-response tasks is not connected to a response execution unit, transient wrong-channel activation never becomes an overt error, so the task difference arises downstream of conflict detection rather than at it.
span.quote: The difference in behavioral profiles across the two tasks is captured in the model by the simple fact that premature activation of the incorrect nontarget decision layer unit does not result in an overt behavior under a one-response task situation.

span.label: The trial-by-trial fit of the model to individual subjects' behaviour is low, which the authors attribute partly to unsimulated human noise processes.
span.note: what this limits: the trial-by-trial fit to individual behaviour: ALTHOUGH THESE NUMBERS INDICATE A SOMEWHAT LOW FIT, NOISE PROCESSES IN HUMANS (WHICH ARE POORLY UNDERSTOOD) MAY MAKE A SIGNIFICANT CONTRIBUTION TO TRIAL-BY-TRIAL BEHAVIORAL PERFORMANCE
span.quote: Although these numbers indicate a somewhat low fit, it is important to note that noise processes in humans (which are poorly understood) may make a significant contribution to trialby-trial behavioral performance.

span.label: The imaging reanalysis testing the sequence prediction was hampered by hemodynamic overlap in rapid event-related fMRI.
span.note: what this limits: the imaging test of the sequence prediction: THIS ANALYSIS WAS COMPLICATED BY OUR USE OF RAPID EVENT-RELATED fMRI AND THE SLOW EVOLUTION OF THE HEMODYNAMIC RESPONSE
span.quote: This analysis was complicated by our use of rapid event-related fMRI and the slow evolution of the hemodynamic response.

span.label: The model covers only a specific type of control, not cognitive control in general.
span.note: what this limits: the model's coverage, bounded by the authors: THE PRESENT STUDY WAS NOT INTENDED TO PROVIDE A COMPLETE ACCOUNT OF THE MYRIAD PROCESSES THAT CONTRIBUTE TO COGNITIVE CONTROL
span.quote: The present study was not intended to provide a complete account of the myriad processes that contribute to cognitive control.

span.label: response conflict
span.quote: Specifically, conflict theory suggests that the ACC detects conflict between different response tendencies.

span.label: anterior cingulate cortex
span.quote: indicates that the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) detects the presence of response conflict and conveys this information to other brain regions, enabling subsequent adjustments in cognitive control.

span.label: cognitive control
span.quote: indicates that the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) detects the presence of response conflict and conveys this information to other brain regions, enabling subsequent adjustments in cognitive control.

span.label: conflict model
span.quote: In order to test this idea, however, existing implementations of the conflict model had to be augmented so as to be responsive to the effects of stimulus frequency on processing.

span.label: **THE MECHANISM IS A CHAIN OF THREE VERBS AND EACH ONE IS DOING WORK:** the ACC `DETECTS the presence of response conflict and CONVEYS this information to other brain regions, enabling subsequent ADJUSTMENTS IN COGNITIVE CONTROL`. Detect, convey, adjust. **A claim that a region is `active during` something cannot be wrong in an interesting way; this one can** - it predicts that the signal precedes the adjustment, that removing it removes the adjustment, and that its size tracks the amount of competition rather than the difficulty
span.quote: indicates that the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) detects the presence of response conflict and conveys this information to other brain regions, enabling subsequent adjustments in cognitive control.

span.label: **AND IT MEETS erb2019 HEAD-ON WITHOUT EITHER PAPER KNOWING.** This model predicts `the dynamics of ACC activity related to TRIAL SEQUENCE EFFECTS` - performance on a trial depending on whether the previous one conflicted, which is the congruency sequence effect. **erb2019, merged into this corpus this morning, finds that associative priming overlap decides whether a CSE is evidence of control at all.** So the corpus holds the computational account and the paper questioning what its central evidence measures, seventeen years apart, neither citing the other. **This sense was first attached to the conflict-theory sentence, which does not contain the words `trial sequence effects` at all** - the audit caught it before the gate did, which is the one step in this pipeline that has no automated equivalent
span.quote: In addition, the model captured detailed aspects of behavioral reaction time and accuracy data, predicted the dynamics of ACC activity related to trial sequence effects, and provided evidence for the functional role of conflict information in performance monitoring and optimization.

span.label: **THE ORDER OF EVENTS IS REPORTED HONESTLY, WHICH IS RARER THAN IT SHOULD BE:** `In order to test this idea, however, EXISTING IMPLEMENTATIONS OF THE CONFLICT MODEL HAD TO BE AUGMENTED so as to be responsive to the effects of stimulus frequency on processing.` The model did not handle frequency; it was extended; then it fitted. **A model extended to fit the data it then fits is a weaker result than one that predicted it**, and stating the sequence lets a reader price that difference instead of having to reconstruct it from the methods
span.quote: In order to test this idea, however, existing implementations of the conflict model had to be augmented so as to be responsive to the effects of stimulus frequency on processing.

span.label: extends → Cho et al. (2002) sequential-priming choice-discrimination model
span.quote: The present model extends this previous work by adding the conflict-control loop (Botvinick et al., 2001) into the Cho et al. model.

span.label: builds-on → Usher and McClelland (2001) leaky competing accumulator architecture
span.quote: As was mentioned above, the basic architecture was developed in Usher and McClelland (2001) and was extended by Botvinick et al. (2001) and Cho et al. (2002).

span.label: builds-on → Braver, Barch, Gray, Molfese, and Snyder (2001) neuroimaging dataset
span.quote: The neuroimaging data used for the present study were originally reported in Braver et al. (2001).

span.label: anterior cingulate cortex —operationalised-as→ response conflict
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — **BUILT FROM THE CHAIN SENTENCE, NOT THE THEORY ONE, AND THE REASON IS AN ABBREVIATION.** `Specifically, conflict theory suggests that the ACC detects conflict between different response tendencies` is the cleaner statement of this relation - and it writes `ACC`, while the node is `anterior cingulate cortex`. The endpoint rule refused it. **Fifth edge tonight lost or moved on wording**, and this one is the most ordinary of them: a paper defines an abbreviation once and then uses it, which every paper does. So the relation comes from the sentence that spells the region out. The DIRECTION is the careful part either way: the ACC does not CAUSE conflict - conflict is a property of the response system and the ACC is where it is read off, which is why ACC activity serves as a conflict measure throughout the imaging literature. Weight 0.9 because `operationalised-as` is my reading of `detects`; the paper does not say the region IS the measure, it says the region detects.
span.quote: indicates that the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) detects the presence of response conflict and conveys this information to other brain regions, enabling subsequent adjustments in cognitive control.

span.label: response conflict —causes→ cognitive control
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.95 — **THIS IS THE WHOLE ACCOUNT IN ONE TRIPLE AND IT IS THE STRONGER OF THE TWO.** `enabling subsequent ADJUSTMENTS IN COGNITIVE CONTROL` - conflict is detected, and control changes as a result. Weight 0.95: both endpoints named as words, the causal direction is explicit in `enabling subsequent`, and the sentence is the paper's summary of an established body of evidence rather than a hedge. **The ACC sits between the two endpoints in the same sentence and is deliberately not in this triple** - it is the route, not a term of the relation, and putting it in would make a three-place claim into a two-place one and lose which part is which.
span.quote: indicates that the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) detects the presence of response conflict and conveys this information to other brain regions, enabling subsequent adjustments in cognitive control.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: displaying a parallel trend of performance decline for low-frequency events when compared against either high-frequency [RT, F(1,63) = 3,771, p , .001; accuracy, F(1,63) = 2,563, p , .001]

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Model and behavioral data were compared across sequential categories through a 16-point correlation coefficient.

span.label: partial correlation
span.quote: The ability of the intact model to account for additional variation in the trial-by-trial reaction time and error rates of individual subjects beyond that accounted for by the lesioned model was calculated as a partial correlation.

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: The average trial-by-trial correlation between the model and the subject data was .412 (99% confidence interval; .389–.435) for RT and was .254 (99% confidence interval; .225–.283) for errors

span.label: standard score (z score)
span.quote: RTs were expressed as z scores, whereas error data were expressed as a difference from that subject’s mean accuracy rate

span.label: t-test
span.quote: There were significant adjustments in RT following errors [t(60) = 6.50, p , .001], in error rate following slow RT trials [t(64) = 25.76, p , .001], and in both RT and error rate following fast RT trials [RT, t(64) = 22.6, p , .01; error rate, t(64) = 4.81, p , .001].

span.label: p-value
span.quote: There was significantly greater conflict for low- versus high-frequency events in all task conditions (all ps , .001).

span.label: mean
span.quote: mean RT and percentage of error were calculated across subjects (both actual and simulated) for each frequency condition

span.label: The simulated conflict measure was higher on low-frequency trials in every task condition, matching the ACC imaging result.
span.quote: There was significantly greater conflict for low- versus high-frequency events in all task conditions (all ps , .001).

span.label: The model reproduced the puzzling exception that accuracy to low-frequency targets in the oddball (one-response) task is near perfect and not degraded by low frequency.
span.quote: In this condition, low-frequency responses were nearly perfectly accurate and were not significantly different from responses to high-frequency [F(1,63) = 0.297, p = .588] or equal-frequency [F(1,63) = 0.133, p = .717] events.

span.label: Simulated conflict tracked not only global stimulus frequency but the fine-grained five-trial sequential history of stimuli.
span.quote: The high correlation observed between conflict and empirical data behavioral performance (accuracy, r = .934; RT, r = .891) indicates that conflict not only tracks global frequency but also the local sequential history of stimuli.

span.label: A reanalysis of the imaging data confirmed the model's novel prediction that ACC activity fluctuates with local sequence even under globally equal frequencies.
span.quote: the empirical data from the ACC corresponds rather well with the conflict predictions obtained from the model (r = .856, p , .001), accounting for 73% of the variance present in the sequential pattern of ACC activation

span.label: Trials whose four preceding stimuli were repetitions had the fastest reaction times and fewest errors, in both human and simulated data.
span.quote: In fact, the four categories ending in RR had the four lowest RTs and error rates in both the behavioral and the simulated data.

span.label: Removing the conflict-monitoring control loop degraded the model's ability to predict trial-by-trial performance, showing the loop makes a real contribution.
span.quote: The performance of the model with no conflictmonitoring control loop was slightly less effective at predicting performance, thus indicating a contribution of this component of the model.

span.label: Subjects showed speed-accuracy adjustments after slow (high-conflict) trials as well as after errors, exactly as the intact conflict-control model predicted.
span.quote: There were significant adjustments in RT following errors [t(60) = 6.50, p , .001], in error rate following slow RT trials [t(64) = 25.76, p , .001], and in both RT and error rate following fast RT trials [RT, t(64) = 22.6, p , .01; error rate, t(64) = 4.81, p , .001].

span.label: response conflict (as simultaneous coactivation of incompatible responses)
span.term: response conflict (as simultaneous coactivation of incompatible responses)
span.quote: Conflict can be thought of as the simultaneous coactivation of incompatible responses, such as trying to name the ink color of the word “red” written in green ink in the classic Stroop task.

span.label: response conflict (origin in constraints on response generation)
span.term: response conflict (origin in constraints on response generation)
span.quote: Response conflict arises because of either physical or task-induced constraints on response generation.

span.label: repetition priming and alternation priming
span.quote: This priming came in two forms: (1) repetition priming (facilitation of a given stimulus after that stimulus had previously been observed) and (2) alternation priming (facilitation of the stimulus opposite to that last observed, following a previous alternation).

span.label: conflict (computational measure based on the Hopfield energy)
span.term: conflict (computational measure based on the Hopfield energy)
span.quote: Conflict was computed as in previous simulations (Botvinick et al., 2001) and corresponded to a simplified form of the well-known Hopfield energy measure (Hopfield, 1982).

span.label: stimulus frequency (low / equal / high)
span.quote: we suggest that the tasks tap a common factor, stimulus frequency, that modulates the degree of conflict present on any given trial.

span.label: task type (one-response go/no-go and oddball vs two-response 2AFC)
span.term: task type (one-response go/no-go and oddball vs two-response 2AFC)
span.quote: The subjects performed two types of speeded response tasks: one-response (go/no-go/oddball) and two-response (2AFC).

span.label: local sequential history (repetition/alternation category over the previous five trials)
span.term: local sequential history (repetition/alternation category over the previous five trials)
span.quote: Analyses of data were conducted after categorizing each stimulus as a function of the previous five trials

span.label: reaction time and error rate
span.quote: mean RT and percentage of error were calculated across subjects (both actual and simulated) for each frequency condition

span.label: ACC activity (peak event-related amplitude in the ACC region of interest)
span.term: ACC activity (peak event-related amplitude in the ACC region of interest)
span.quote: ACC activation was expressed in terms of the difference between the low- and the highfrequency responses; for equal-frequency conditions, one stimulus was arbitrarily chosen as the baseline.

span.label: simulated conflict index
span.quote: Mean simulated conflict for each stimulus was also calculated as a function of frequency and task condition for comparison against imaging data from the ACC

span.label: lesioned model (strategic priming fixed at its mean, conflict-control loop removed)
span.term: lesioned model (strategic priming fixed at its mean, conflict-control loop removed)
span.quote: The first was with the intact model, whereas the second was with the strategic priming mechanism (which modulates control as a function of conflict) lesioned.

span.label: 65 subjects / 14 subjects — sample sizes of the behavioral and the neuroimaging studies whose data the simulations were fitted to
span.quote: There were 65 subjects (47 females and 18 males; mean age, 19.3 years; range, 17 –25 years) in the behavioral study and 14 subjects (5 males and 9 females; mean age, 22.9 years; range, 18–27 years) in the neuroimaging study.

span.label: 17%, 50%, 83% — the three target-frequency conditions used in each version of the task
span.quote: Each version of the task (one-response, two-response) had three frequency conditions: low-frequency target/R1 (target = 17%), equalfrequency (target = 50%), and low-frequency nontarget/ R2 (target = 83%).

span.label: r = .856 ... 73% — correlation between simulated conflict and reanalyzed ACC activity across matched sequence pairs, and the share of variance it explains
span.quote: the empirical data from the ACC corresponds rather well with the conflict predictions obtained from the model (r = .856, p , .001), accounting for 73% of the variance present in the sequential pattern of ACC activation

span.label: 16.6% / 6.8% — variance in trial-by-trial reaction time and in error explained by the full model
span.quote: the model accounts for 16.6% of the variance present in the RT and 6.8% of the variance present in error

span.label: 2.5% / 1.5% — the small but reliable extra variance attributable specifically to the conflict-control loop
span.quote: Thus, although the conflictcontrol effect was rather small—accounting for 2.5% of the total variation in the subjects’ RT scores and 1.5% of variance in error rates—it was highly reliable.

span.label: 64 out of 65 — subjects for whom adding the conflict-control loop improved the model's RT prediction
span.quote: This partial correlation was computed separately for each subject and was positive for 64 out of 65 subjects in the RT analysis (mean partial correlation = .141; 99% confidence

span.label: F(1,63) = 9,143 — test that the low-vs-high frequency conflict difference exceeded the difference under equal frequency
span.quote: the conflict difference between low- and high-frequency stimuli was significantly greater than the difference between stimulus types under equalfrequency conditions [F(1,63) = 9,143, p , .001].
